title: Sessionized Loadbench Casebook and Instability Heuristics
content:
Purpose:
A practical casebook of observed instability modes in our throughput harness when session affinity and client sessionization are used. This is a working log + heuristics list intended for engineers running mid-to-long benchmarking runs (10m–6h) against the serving runtime. The goal is to improve repeatability without compromising realism for sessioned workloads (chat-style, KV-cache heavy flows).

Background and motivation:
- Many of our existing docs focus on warmup and priming, but we've seen a class of intermittent run failures and throughput drift that correlate with sessionization and client affinity policies.
- Sessionized workloads exercise KV cache, attention cache eviction, and backend affinity differently than purely stateless fanout. Small differences in client scheduling or RNG can cascade into large throughput variance.

Key observations (casebook entries):
1) Sticky-client tail drift (Observed 2024-11):
   - Symptom: 10–20% throughput drop after ~35–50m, not correlated with CPU/GPU temperature.
   - Root cause hypothesis: session key clustering caused uneven KV cache occupancy; some partitions experience higher hit rates while others thrash, increasing average latency and reducing effective concurrency.
   - Mitigation: enforce session shard rebalancing every N requests in the harness; randomize initial session-key assignment to avoid long-lived hot shards.

2) Microburst GC stalls in Python harness (Observed 2024-12):
   - Symptom: sub-second pauses in the load generator that manifest as increased jitter and occasional request timeouts.
   - Root cause: periodic reference cycles and memory churn in the client driver (python asyncio loop + large prompt buffers).
   - Mitigation: pin the loadgen to PyPy for long runs or run the generator in multiple short-lived processes; add explicit gc.collect() at controlled cadence in between ramp phases.

3) KV-cache fragmentation after mixed-length prompts (Observed 2025-01):
   - Symptom: initially good throughput, then sudden reduction in tokens/sec when short and long prompts are interleaved without warmup.
   - Root cause: runtime's per-session cache maps fragmented under mixed sequence lengths, causing inefficient kernel selection and additional memcpy overhead.
   - Mitigation: warmup with a sample distribution that mirrors expected sequence-length histogram; include synthetic long-context primers to condition kernel paths.

Harness design recommendations (session-aware):
- Session lifecycle: model sessions explicitly in the harness. Each virtual client maintains a session id, kv state marker, and local RNG seed. Session churn and session-stickiness must be configurable.
- Two-tier warmup: (1) Session priming stage: for each session, replay N short prompts and a few long primers to populate the KV cache; (2) Global runtime warmup: ramp global QPS across all sessions to target concurrency to stabilize scheduling.
- Session churn knob: parameterize session-ttl and churn-rate. For repeatability runs, use deterministic churn schedule (seeded RNG) and capture the seed.
- Anchor requests: reserve a small percentage (1–2%) of requests as 'anchors' (fixed prompts) to provide stable latency and quality baselines across runs. Always include anchor responses in artifacts.

Warmup recipe (practical):
1) Cold-start baseline: 2m monitoring-only to capture cold allocation costs.
2) Session priming: for each session, send 3 short prompts (seq_len 16–32), 1 medium (128), and 1 long primer (512) spaced at 150–300ms.
3) Occupancy ramp: over 8–12 minutes, increase client concurrency linearly to target concurrency; watch rolling 1m throughput and 95/99 latencies.
4) Hold at target for 10–30 minutes to detect slow drift before starting main measurement window.

Repeatability anchors and metadata capture (must be automatic):
- RNG seed(s) for session assignment and request sampling (store every run).
- Client binary/commit hash and container image tags.
- Loadgen node list/ip, timezone, and NTP sync status.
- GPU driver, CUDA, cuDNN, and kernel versions.
- nvml snapshots (util, mem used) every 10s and at run start/end.
- Tracing ids for 1p request traces (sampled at 0.1% or 1 in 1000).
- Anchored prompt responses (hash of output) for golden-check.

Instrumentation checklist (minimal):
- Host: top/htop, iostat, vmstat, dstat, network tx/rx at 1s granularity for first 5m, then 10s.
- GPU: nvidia-smi / nvml telemetry every 5s; collect per-GPU PCIe bandwidth if supported.
- Kernel: perf counters for scheduler latency, memcpy hotspots, and kernel launch queuing (sampled during heat window).
- Runtime: internal perf events (KV hit/miss counters, attention kernel selection counts, active-session histogram).
- Client: queue length, per-session outstanding requests, retry counts, and internal loop GC stats.

Experiment matrix (examples):
- Axis A (sessionization): static stickiness / churn-rate 0.01 / churn-rate 0.1 / fully stateless
- Axis B (prompt mix): homogeneous short / mixed / long-heavy
- Axis C (warmup style): no warmup / session priming only / two-stage warmup (recommended)
- Axis D (client topology): single loadgen node / multi-node spread / multi-process per node
Run each cell 3x with different seeds, include postmortem diff across anchors.

Common failure modes and remediation heuristics:
- Gradual throughput decline without resource saturation: suspect KV eviction hotspots or scheduler backpressure. Capture per-session cache occupancy and re-run with increased session priming.
- High variance across repeats: check RNG seed capture and loadgen clock skew; prefer multi-run median not mean.
- Occasional long tail spikes: trace and correlate with nvml-power or host interrupts; if correlated to thermal cycles, add temperature stabilization and extend ramp time.
- Run-to-run non-determinism in microbench loops: ensure driver versions match and disable experimental kernel selection if evaluating baseline.

Post-run artifacts to collect automatically:
- aggregated throughput/latency CSVs (1s resolution), per-session latency percentiles, and anchor-response hashes
- nvml logs, perf traces, and a sampled flamegraph for the busiest 60s window
- loadgen stdout/stderr, client GC logs, and process-level memmaps
- small human-readable run summary (2–4 bullet paragraphs) explaining anomalies and suspected root causes

Quick run checklist (preflight):
- [ ] Confirm NTP sync and identical timezone across loadgen nodes
- [ ] Bake loadgen image with commit tag and note hash in run metadata
- [ ] Verify session-key distribution seed present in config
- [ ] Ensure anchors are present and configured to be stored
- [ ] Start nvml capture and perf daemon before loadgen ramp
- [ ] Run short sanity 3m test at 10% of target QPS to validate topology

Notes to engineers (practical tips):
- Prefer multiple short repeated runs with identical seeds over a single very long run when debugging non-determinism. Long runs are useful for thermal and fragmentation effects but harder to triage.
- When reproducing a drift, bisect on session churn first: flip between churned and sticky runs, keep everything else identical.
- Use anchors and golden hashes to quickly tell if outputs diverged; divergence often flags a different kernel path or quantization fallback.
- If you must disable sessionization for a baseline, document it clearly — stateless baselines are useful but not representative for many customer workloads.

Outstanding questions and follow-ups:
- Should we add a harness mode that artificially staggers session priming to simulate real-world chat onboarding patterns? (A: high ROI; tentative implementation in PR linked above.)
- How often should we rotate session-shard mapping during long runs to avoid long-tail hotness without changing semantics? Proposal: rotate at 5–15 minute windows with deterministic seed.
- Can runtime surface a per-session fragmentation metric? Filing a small instrumentation task for the runtime team.

Appendix: quick commands and snippets (examples only)
- Dump nvml every 5s: nvml_logger --interval 5 --out run_nvml.csv
- Start perf capture for 60s busy window: perf record -F 200 -a -g -- sleep 60; perf script | inferno-collapse; flamescope or speedscope ingestion
- Anchor response hashing: sha256sum <(jq -c .response)  # run for each stored anchor

If you reproduce a novel instability, paste a short case entry into this doc with timestamps, seeds, and a minimal repro. This file should be the first search result for anyone chasing session-related throughput drift.
